saint_pick.name: Columbanus
saint_pick.selection_reason: Columbanus has the most vivid, best-documented story of the group: Jonas of Bobbio's near-contemporary Life and his own surviving letters and Rule tell of his exile from Luxeuil by Queen Brunhild, his journey across the Alps and the founding of Bobbio. He is not a household name, his Catholic references are strong, and he is commemorated on this date.
saint_pick.catholic_veneration: Canonized saint (pre-congregation); listed in the Roman Martyrology and kept on 23 November in the Roman liturgical calendar (an optional memorial in the General Roman Calendar and a feast in Ireland), with a cult at Bobbio and Luxeuil.

script.portrait: An Irish abbot in a rough undyed monastic habit with a hood, holding a plain abbot's staff in one hand and an open book in the other, standing alone and facing the viewer. Behind him are dark pine forest and a simple stone monastery chapel under a gold-leaf sky.

beats.text: Driven into exile, he wrote to his monks: "Farewell, dear hearts of mine."
beats.scene: A gaunt Irish abbot in a rough monastic habit stands at a river quay on the Loire, writing on a small parchment while holding it against a ship's rail. Frankish soldiers in sixth-century dress wait nearby, and a wooden sailing ship lies at the quay.

beats.text: Saint Columbanus, Irish monk born in the sixth century, who died at Bobbio, Italy.
He had left Ireland with twelve companions. In the mountains of Burgundy they lived in a ruined Roman fortress, often eating forest herbs, berries and bark.
beats.scene: Twelve monks in rough habits gather herbs and berries among pine trees outside a half-ruined Roman fortress with crumbling stone walls and round arches. Columbanus stands among them with a staff, in the wooded Vosges mountains.

beats.text: So many followed that new monasteries rose. Then he rebuked the young king for keeping a concubine, and the king's grandmother Brunhilda turned against him.
beats.scene: In a Merovingian royal hall with rounded stone arches, a young king in a jeweled tunic sits beside his stern grandmother in a veiled gown and crown. Columbanus, in a plain habit, stands before them with one raised hand, as courtiers look on.

beats.text: A storm drove his ship back to shore. He crossed the Alps, and in Italy a king gave him land at Bobbio for a monastery.
beats.scene: Columbanus and a few monks in hooded habits climb a narrow snowy Alpine pass with walking staffs. Far below, a green valley opens toward distant Italian hills.

beats.text: He spoke plainly to kings, wrote to popes with reverence, and longed for silence.
beats.scene: At Bobbio in the Apennine Mountains, Columbanus sits at a wooden desk with a quill and parchment beside a small stone church. Monks in habits work quietly in the courtyard.

beats.text: Love can cross any distance, even exile. Saint Columbanus, pray for us.

claims.claim: Columbanus was an Irish missionary born in Leinster, c. 543, who founded monasteries in the Frankish and Lombard kingdoms, including Luxeuil and Bobbio.
He died at Bobbio in 615.
He set sail from Ireland with twelve companions.
He settled in the half-ruined Roman fortress of Annegray in the Vosges Mountains, where food was often forest herbs, berries and the bark of young trees.
So many disciples came that Luxeuil and then Fontaines were founded.
King Guntram of Burgundy welcomed him and granted land.
Columbanus rebuked Theuderic II for having a concubine, and Theuderic's grandmother Brunhilda became his bitterest foe.
He was driven toward Ireland by force, and at Nantes wrote to his monks: 'Farewell, dear hearts of mine; pray for me that I may live in God.'
A severe storm drove the ship back ashore soon after it sailed from Nantes.
He crossed the Alps into Lombardy, where King Agilulf granted him land at Bobbio, and he built a monastery there in 614.
He wrote to the Frankish bishops with a mixture of freedom, reverence and charity, asking only to live in silence in the forests.
He wrote to popes with deference, calling the pope his Lord and Father in Christ.
He often withdrew to a cave seven miles away, seeking solitude.
The Frankish bishops disputed his Celtic dating of Easter; the matter appears to end after he left their jurisdiction.
His Rule and penitential teaching emphasised private confession to a priest followed by penances.
Jonas of Bobbio wrote the Life of Columbanus c. 639–643, relying on companions of the saint.
Luxeuil remained active after his expulsion and helped form new monasteries.
The exact year of his birth is uncertain.
Jonas tells that as a young man he took the advice of a religious woman to flee temptation, and that his mother tried to stop him from leaving home.
Pope Benedict XVI named Columbanus patron of motorcyclists in November 2011; he is also patron of Bobbio and of Ireland.
Bobbio became an important centre of written culture; Luxeuil was suppressed in 1790 and Bobbio closed in 1803, and both abbey churches are now parish churches.
His feast is kept on 23 November.

story: Columbanus was born in the Irish kingdom of Leinster. The traditional year is 543, though the exact date is not certain. His name is the Latin form of Colmán, meaning "little dove." Most of what we know comes from his own surviving letters and writings and from the Life written by Jonas, a monk of Bobbio, around 640, drawing on men who had known him.

He was educated under Abbot Sinell, and then at the great monastery of Bangor under Abbot Comgall. He studied Scripture, grammar and rhetoric, and he wrote a commentary on the Psalms. Jonas tells of a young man tormented by temptation, who sought the counsel of a holy woman and chose to leave the world. According to that account, his mother threw herself across the doorway to stop him, and he stepped over her and left. Scholars caution that the story of the holy woman's counsel may be shaped by the spiritual aims of the biography. Around the age of forty, he felt called to preach the Gospel abroad, and Comgall reluctantly agreed.

He set sail with twelve companions, among them Attala and Gall. They crossed to the Continent at a time when, as Jonas describes it, the Christian faith in Gaul had grown thin. Warfare and neglect had weakened it. King Guntram of Burgundy welcomed them and gave them land. They settled in the half-ruined Roman fortress of Annegray in the Vosges Mountains, where they often lived on forest herbs, berries and the bark of young trees. Crowds came, noble and poor, and so many asked to join them that a second monastery was founded at Luxeuil, and then a third at Fontaines. For them Columbanus wrote a Rule, drawn from the customs of Bangor, and taught a way of repentance centred on private confession to a priest.

Even so, he loved solitude. Often he went to a cave about seven miles away, accompanied by one monk who carried messages. In 602 the Frankish bishops summoned him to answer for his Celtic date of Easter and his independence. He did not go. He wrote instead, with what the Catholic Encyclopedia calls a strange mixture of freedom, reverence and charity, asking only: "permit me to live in silence in these forests." He also appealed to the popes, and the dispute seems to have faded once he left their jurisdiction.

His deeper trouble was with the royal court. When he rebuked the young King Theuderic II of Burgundy for keeping a concubine, the king's grandmother Brunhilda, who ruled as regent, turned against him. Columbanus was imprisoned, escaped, and was then driven from Luxeuil by soldiers. Only the monks from Ireland were allowed to go with him. At Nantes, before boarding, he wrote to his brothers: "Farewell, dear hearts of mine; pray for me that I may live in God." He asked them to obey Attala, who stayed behind as abbot. A storm drove the ship back to shore, and the captain refused to sail again. Columbanus found shelter with King Chlothar II and went on to the court of Theudebert II.

Another path opened. He travelled up the Rhine toward the Alps. At Bregenz on Lake Constance a community was founded, and Gall stayed in the region when Columbanus moved on. When war and danger came, he crossed the Alps into Lombardy. In 612 King Agilulf and Queen Theodelinda welcomed him in Milan. He wrote against Arianism, and at the king's request he wrote to Pope Boniface IV with warmth and candour, calling Rome the head of the Churches. In 614 the king gave him land at Bobbio in the Apennines, with a ruined church dedicated to Saint Peter. There Columbanus built his last monastery.

He died at Bobbio in 615. His Rule was later replaced in many places by the gentler Rule of Saint Benedict, but his work did not end with him. Luxeuil carried on after his expulsion and helped found new monasteries. Bobbio became a centre of learning and of written culture. Both abbeys later fell to political upheaval, Luxeuil in 1790 and Bobbio in 1803, yet their churches still stand as parish churches. The Church keeps his feast on 23 November. He is the patron of Bobbio and of Ireland, and in 2011 Pope Benedict XVI named him patron of motorcyclists. His own letters survive, and in them we hear a man who loved the Church, spoke honestly, and kept a heart full of affection for those he left behind.

issues: Close beat had no meaning line (rule: one short line under 12 words, then 'Saint ___, pray for us'). Added 'Love can cross any distance, even exile.' Total is now about 127 words.
Story beat 1: the sources say forest herbs, berries and bark were 'oftentimes' the food, not always. Added 'often'.
youtube_title said 'Exiled by a Queen'. The sources show the exile was ordered by King Theuderic II, with his grandmother Brunhilda as regent and foe, not a reigning queen. Retitled.
share_cta was a little flip ('could use a patron today'). Reworded to a more reverent tone.

Website story: the caution that the tale 'may be shaped by the spiritual aims of the biography' is supported (source 2) only for the temptation and holy-woman episode, not the mother-in-the-doorway detail. Made the reference specific.

es.name: San Columbano
es.hook: Una carta escrita como si un barco esperara en Nantes: la despedida de un monje irlandés que fue alejado de su propia comunidad.
es.summary: San Columbano, monje irlandés, fundó monasterios en Borgoña, fue desterrado tras reprender a un rey y pasó sus últimos años construyendo Bobbio, en Italia.
story: Columbano nació en el reino irlandés de Leinster. El año tradicional es 543, aunque la fecha exacta no es segura. Su nombre es la forma latina de Colmán, que significa «pequeña paloma». La mayor parte de lo que sabemos procede de sus cartas y escritos que se conservan, y de la Vida escrita por Jonás, monje de Bobbio, hacia el año 640, basada en testimonios de hombres que lo habían conocido.

Fue educado bajo el abad Sinell y después en el gran monasterio de Bangor, bajo el abad Comgal. Estudió las Escrituras, la gramática y la retórica, y escribió un comentario sobre los Salmos. Jonás relata la historia de un joven atormentado por la tentación, que buscó el consejo de una mujer santa y decidió abandonar el mundo. Según ese relato, su madre se arrojó sobre el umbral para detenerlo, y él pasó por encima de ella y se marchó. Los estudiosos advierten que el relato del consejo de la mujer santa puede estar moldeado por los propósitos espirituales de la biografía. Hacia los cuarenta años, sintió la llamada a predicar el Evangelio en tierras lejanas, y Comgal accedió a regañadientes.

Se hizo a la mar con doce compañeros, entre ellos Atala y Galo. Cruzaron al continente en una época en que, según describe Jonás, la fe cristiana en la Galia se había debilitado. La guerra y el abandono la habían enflaquecido. El rey Gontrán de Borgoña los acogió y les dio tierras. Se establecieron en la fortaleza romana medio en ruinas de Annegray, en los montes Vosgos, donde a menudo vivían de hierbas del bosque, bayas y corteza de árboles jóvenes. Acudían multitudes, nobles y pobres, y tantos pedían unirse a ellos que se fundó un segundo monasterio en Luxeuil y luego un tercero en Fontaines. Para ellos Columbano escribió una Regla, inspirada en las costumbres de Bangor, y enseñó un camino de penitencia centrado en la confesión privada ante un sacerdote.

Aun así, amaba la soledad. Con frecuencia iba a una cueva a unos once kilómetros de distancia, acompañado de un solo monje que llevaba los mensajes. En el año 602, los obispos francos lo convocaron para responder por la fecha celta de la Pascua y por su independencia. No acudió. En cambio, escribió con lo que la Enciclopedia Católica llama una extraña mezcla de libertad, reverencia y caridad, pidiendo solamente: «permitidme vivir en silencio en estos bosques». También apeló a los papas, y la disputa parece haberse apagado una vez que salió de su jurisdicción.

Su mayor problema fue con la corte real. Cuando reprendió al joven rey Teoderico II de Borgoña por mantener una concubina, la abuela del rey, Brunequilda, que gobernaba como regente, se volvió contra él. Columbano fue encarcelado, escapó y después fue expulsado de Luxeuil por soldados. Solo se permitió que los monjes irlandeses lo acompañaran. En Nantes, antes de embarcar, escribió a sus hermanos: «Adiós, queridos corazones míos; rogad por mí para que pueda vivir en Dios». Les pidió que obedecieran a Atala, quien se quedó como abad. Una tormenta devolvió el barco a la orilla, y el capitán se negó a zarpar de nuevo. Columbano encontró refugio con el rey Clotario II y continuó hasta la corte de Teodeberto II.

Se abrió otro camino. Remontó el Rin hacia los Alpes. En Bregenz, junto al lago de Constanza, se fundó una comunidad, y Galo permaneció en la región cuando Columbano se marchó. Cuando llegaron la guerra y el peligro, cruzó los Alpes hacia Lombardía. En el año 612, el rey Agilulfo y la reina Teodelinda lo recibieron en Milán. Escribió contra el arrianismo y, a petición del rey, escribió al papa Bonifacio IV con calidez y franqueza, llamando a Roma cabeza de las Iglesias. En el año 614, el rey le concedió tierras en Bobbio, en los Apeninos, junto a una iglesia en ruinas dedicada a San Pedro. Allí Columbano construyó su último monasterio.

Murió en Bobbio en el año 615. Su Regla fue reemplazada en muchos lugares por la Regla más suave de San Benito, pero su obra no terminó con él. Luxeuil continuó después de su expulsión y ayudó a fundar nuevos monasterios. Bobbio se convirtió en un centro de saber y de cultura escrita. Ambas abadías sufrieron después las convulsiones políticas, Luxeuil en 1790 y Bobbio en 1803, pero sus iglesias siguen en pie como iglesias parroquiales. La Iglesia celebra su fiesta el 23 de noviembre. Es patrono de Bobbio y de Irlanda, y en 2011 el papa Benedicto XVI lo declaró patrono de los motociclistas. Sus cartas se conservan, y en ellas escuchamos a un hombre que amó a la Iglesia, habló con honestidad y guardó un corazón lleno de afecto por quienes dejó atrás.
es.prayer: El amor puede cruzar cualquier distancia, incluso el destierro. San Columbano, ruega por nosotros.
